questions.question_text: Which organism is implicated in Prion disease?
questions.explanation: Fatal Familial Insomnia is a human prion disease, along with others like sCJD, vCJD, Kuru, and Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker syndrome.

questions.question_text: A 75-year-old man has gradually changed in personality and behaviour over the last year with notably poor memory. His initial serological investigations are unremarkable. He has autonomic instability of heart rate and blood pressure and has experienced falls due to sudden 'jerks' in his legs associated with pain. His MRI shows mildly increased T2-FLAIR signaling in the medial temporal lobes. Which antibodies/antigens are implicated?
questions.explanation: The autonomic instability and 'jerks' (peripheral nerve hyperexcitability) are suggestive of CASPR2-mediated autoimmune encephalitis, with T2-FLAIR involvement of medial temporal lobes indicating limbic encephalitis.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man with schizophrenia (not currently on antipsychotics) presents with a 3-day history of mutism and immobility. On examination, he has fever (39.5°C), tachycardia (125 bpm), fluctuating blood pressure, profound muscle rigidity, and maintains unusual postures when positioned (catalepsy). He actively resists passive movements (negativism). Blood tests show creatine kinase of 15,000 U/L and white cell count of 14 × 10⁹/L. He appears alert but does not respond to commands. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Malignant catatonia: fever, autonomic instability, rigidity, elevated CK, plus catatonic features (catalepsy, negativism, mutism) without neuroleptic exposure.

questions.question_text: A 14-year-old female took an overdose of paracetamol after a fight with her boyfriend, presenting with red face, tongue, confusion, and MMSE of 21/30. Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?
questions.explanation: The acute onset of confusion with altered cognition (MMSE 21/30) and physical signs (red face, tongue changes) following overdose is consistent with delirium.

questions.question_text: Which of the following differentiates hypomania from mania?
questions.explanation: The key differentiating feature is the presence of psychotic symptoms (delusions or hallucinations) in mania but not in hypomania. Other features like decreased sleep need, flight of ideas, and increased goal-directed activity occur in both conditions.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT seen in serotonin syndrome?
questions.explanation: Diplopia (double vision) is not a characteristic feature of serotonin syndrome. Common features include neuromuscular abnormalities (tremor, rigidity), autonomic instability (tachycardia, hyperthermia), and altered mental status.

questions.question_text: What is the key distinguishing feature between food restrictive disorder and anorexia nervosa?

options.text: Preoccupation with body weight or shape

correct_answer.text: Preoccupation with body weight or shape

questions.explanation: Food restrictive disorder differs from anorexia nervosa in that the pattern of eating behavior is NOT motivated by preoccupation with body weight or shape, whereas anorexia nervosa explicitly involves desire for thinness or fear of weight gain.

questions.question_text: A patient whose medical tests confirm serious illness says 'Everyone around me seems worried and depressed, but I'm perfectly happy and fine.' What defense mechanism is being used?
questions.explanation: Denial is the refusal to acknowledge the reality of a situation. The patient is denying their illness and its emotional impact.

questions.question_text: A patient absent from therapy for ten days writes a letter stating she doesn't need therapy anymore. Which defense mechanism is most likely being used?
questions.explanation: Rationalization is the most likely defense mechanism, as the patient is creating a logical explanation for her absence and cessation of therapy. Denial would be the most appropriate answer if it were an option, but among the given choices, rationalization best describes the creation of a justifiable reason for discontinuing treatment.

questions.question_text: Which finding is specific to the binge/purge pattern of anorexia nervosa?
questions.explanation: Repeated vomiting in the binge/purge pattern causes salivary gland hypertrophy, particularly of the parotid glands, leading to characteristic parotid swelling.

questions.question_text: In Lewy body dementia, alpha-synuclein accumulation occurs primarily in which of the following brain regions?

options.text: Temporal lobe, cingulate gyrus, frontal lobes, and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

correct_answer.text: Temporal lobe, cingulate gyrus, frontal lobes, and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

questions.explanation: Alpha-synuclein accumulation in Lewy body dementia occurs in the temporal lobe, cingulate gyrus, frontal lobes, and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus.

questions.question_text: Speech disturbance in schizophrenia
questions.explanation: Metonymy is a speech disturbance common in schizophrenia where the affected person uses a word or phrase related to the proper one but not ordinarily used, such as referring to losing the 'piece of string' instead of the 'thread' of conversation.

questions.question_text: In a box-and-whisker plot, what do the upper and lower edges of the box indicate?
questions.explanation: In a box-and-whisker plot, the upper and lower edges of the box represent the interquartile range (IQR), which spans from the 25th percentile to the 75th percentile, containing the middle 50% of the data.

questions.question_text: Which protein pathology is most commonly found in frontotemporal dementia?

options.text: Ubiquitin and tau positive, amyloid negative
All three pathologies in equal amounts

correct_answer.text: Ubiquitin and tau positive, amyloid negative

questions.explanation: Frontotemporal dementia is most commonly associated with ubiquitin-positive and amyloid-negative pathology, followed by tau-positive and amyloid-negative, with Pick's disease showing both tau and ubiquitin positivity.

questions.question_text: What is the most effective treatment for HIV encephalitis?
questions.explanation: Prompt administration of antiretroviral therapy is the most effective treatment for HIV encephalitis, addressing the underlying viral infection causing neurocognitive dysfunction.

questions.question_text: Coiled bodies are pathological inclusions characteristically seen in which condition?
questions.explanation: Coiled bodies are neurofibrillary tangles and tau inclusions found in astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, particularly in the substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus, and globus pallidus. These are characteristic microscopic findings in progressive supranuclear palsy, a rare disorder affecting gait, balance, mood, and cognition.

questions.question_text: Which medication is given for REM sleep behavior disorder?
questions.explanation: While prazosin, trazodone, and melatonin are used for REM sleep behavior disorder, clonazepam is a first-line treatment. Other options include carbamazepine, levodopa, imipramine, and pramipexole.

questions.question_text: What is the IQ range for moderate learning disability?
questions.explanation: Moderate learning disability is defined by an IQ of 35-49 (approximately 35-55). Mild learning disability ranges from 50-70, severe from 20-34, and profound is below 20.

questions.question_text: Which CSF biomarker is decreased in Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: Amyloid-beta 42 is decreased in Alzheimer's disease CSF due to deposition in amyloid plaques in the brain.

questions.question_text: A doctor wants to conduct a systematic review and needs to follow appropriate reporting guidelines. Which reporting guideline should be used?
questions.explanation: PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) is the standard for reporting systematic reviews.

questions.question_text: Nightmares are characterized by:

options.text: Awakening in fear without dream recall
Awakening with vivid recall of frightening dream content

correct_answer.text: Awakening with vivid recall of frightening dream content

questions.explanation: Nightmares are disturbing dreams from which the person awakens with clear memory of the dream content; they occur during REM sleep.

questions.question_text: A man whose friend died in a motorcycle accident now has a paralyzed arm despite no neurological abnormalities found, most likely has
questions.explanation: This presentation is consistent with dissociative neurological symptom disorder (formerly conversion disorder in DSM-5), characterized by motor symptoms (paralysis) inconsistent with recognized neurological disease and related to psychological stress.

questions.question_text: A patient on admission is found to have a suspicious mass on routine chest X-ray, and the medical team decides not to tell him. Which ethical principle best describes this approach?
questions.explanation: Paternalism in medical ethics refers to healthcare professionals making decisions for patients without their explicit consent, often believing such decisions are in the patient's best interests. Not disclosing the suspicious finding is a paternalistic approach, overriding the patient's autonomy.

questions.question_text: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder is characterized by

options.text: Not preoccupied by weight; excludes certain food groups from diet
Binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors
Excessive exercise to compensate for food intake

correct_answer.text: Not preoccupied by weight; excludes certain food groups from diet

questions.explanation: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) is characterized by restriction of foods without the weight or shape concerns seen in anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa. Patients simply exclude certain food groups from their diet.

questions.question_text: Wernicke's aphasia is characterized as which type of aphasia?

options.text: Global aphasia with total loss of language

questions.explanation: Wernicke's aphasia is fluent (output is fluent) but with impaired receptive/comprehension abilities.

questions.question_text: A high-performing student takes alcohol to be able to do a presentation in public. This is indicative of which condition?
questions.explanation: Social phobia is the same as social anxiety disorder in ICD-11. This student is using alcohol to cope with anxiety related to public performance/presentation, which is a characteristic feature of social phobia.

questions.question_text: What percentage of total sleep time is spent in REM sleep?
questions.explanation: REM sleep constitutes approximately 20–25% of total sleep time in normal adults, making C (25%) the correct answer. This is directly stated in the New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry (p.970) a

questions.question_text: Risk factors for autism spectrum disorder include which of the following?

options.text: Maternal use of valproate in pregnancy

questions.explanation: Autism spectrum disorder has a strong genetic basis with heritability around 90%. Multiple risk factors have been identified including sibling with autism, birth defects including cerebral palsy, gestational age less than 35 weeks, and maternal use of valproate in pregnancy. Premature birth and maternal smoking are also recognized risk factors.

questions.question_text: A clinician compares the epidemiology of eating disorders. Which statement about AN and BN prevalence is correct?

options.text: AN is more prevalent than BN
BN is more prevalent than AN
BN is twice as common as AN

correct_answer.text: BN is more prevalent than AN

questions.explanation: Bulimia nervosa (1-2%) is more prevalent than anorexia nervosa (0.5-1%). Both are more common in females.

questions.question_text: What is the best management for HIV-related cognitive impairment?
questions.explanation: Antiretroviral therapy targeting viral replication is the best management for HIV-related cognitive impairment, as it reduces CNS viral load and improves cognitive function.

questions.question_text: A qualitative researcher stops recruiting participants when no new themes emerge from interviews. What concept does this represent?
questions.explanation: Data saturation occurs when additional data collection yields no new information or themes - the point at which recruitment can stop.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman with generalized anxiety disorder has been taking sertraline 200mg daily for 12 weeks with minimal improvement. Her symptoms significantly impair her daily functioning. Which medication is most appropriate to add as augmentation?
questions.explanation: Pregabalin is licensed for GAD and effective augmentation when SSRIs inadequate.

questions.question_text: What type of aura is typical for temporal lobe seizures?
questions.explanation: The most common auras in temporal lobe seizures are abdominal/epigastric sensations (described as butterflies in the stomach or a rising sensation) and psychic auras such as fear, déjà vu, or jamais vu. Auras precede temporal lobe seizures in approximately 80% of cases.

questions.question_text: According to NICE guidelines, a child who has failed fluoxetine treatment for depression should be offered which of the following?

options.text: A different SSRI or another class of antidepressant

correct_answer.text: A different SSRI or another class of antidepressant

questions.explanation: NICE guidelines recommend that if a child fails to respond to one SSRI like fluoxetine, an alternative SSRI such as sertraline or a different class of antidepressant such as venlafaxine or clomipramine should be considered before escalating to other interventions.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is correct regarding separation anxiety disorder?
questions.explanation: Separation anxiety disorder requires a duration of at least 6 months for diagnosis; while it typically begins in childhood, the minimum duration criterion is a key diagnostic feature.

questions.question_text: Which of the following describes locked-in syndrome?

options.text: Complete loss of consciousness with preserved brainstem reflexes
Inability to speak due to motor cortex damage
Total paralysis below the level of the third nerve nuclei with ability to open eyes voluntarily and move eyes vertically
Loss of all eye movements with preserved limb function

correct_answer.text: Total paralysis below the level of the third nerve nuclei with ability to open eyes voluntarily and move eyes vertically

questions.explanation: Locked-in syndrome results from ventral pontine lesions and describes total paralysis below the level of the third nerve nuclei, but patients can open their eyes voluntarily and elevate or depress their eyes to command, while horizontal eye movements are usually lost.

questions.question_text: A dementia screening test identifies 80 true positives and misses 20 patients who actually have dementia. What is the formula for sensitivity?
questions.explanation: Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN). It measures the proportion of actual positives correctly identified.

questions.question_text: Which of the following protein inclusion profiles is most common in frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation: The most common protein inclusion profile in frontotemporal dementia is tau-positive, amyloid-negative, though ubiquitin-positive inclusions are also frequently observed; familial FTD is typically ubiquitin-positive and tau-negative.

questions.question_text: A woman presents with multiple gynecological and gastrointestinal complaints over 10 years. All investigations have been normal, yet she remains convinced that doctors have missed something serious. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?
questions.explanation: Bodily distress disorder is characterized by persistent bodily symptoms that are distressing to the individual with excessive attention directed toward the symptoms. Key features include multiple symptoms varying over time, excessive attention not alleviated by appropriate clinical examination and reassurance, and symptoms present on most days for several months with at least some impact on functioning.

questions.question_text: A patient cannot perform a complex task like using a hammer but can perform each individual step. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Ideational apraxia is the inability to follow a sequence of actions in correct order, such as taking a match from a box and striking it properly.

questions.question_text: A researcher compares types of literature reviews. What distinguishes a systematic review from a narrative review?
questions.explanation: Systematic reviews use explicit and reproducible methods for searching, selecting, and synthesizing evidence. Narrative reviews are more subjective and less structured.

questions.question_text: Confabulation is most characteristically seen in which condition?
questions.explanation: Confabulation occurs in Korsakoff syndrome, where patients unconsciously fill memory gaps with fabricated information.

questions.question_text: A patient with specific phobia undergoes therapy involving progressive exposure to feared stimuli while maintaining relaxation. What therapy involves creating an anxiety hierarchy?
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitization involves creating an anxiety hierarchy and gradually exposing the patient to feared stimuli while paired with relaxation techniques (reciprocal inhibition).

questions.question_text: A high-performing student using alcohol to facilitate public speaking presentations most likely has which anxiety disorder?
questions.explanation: Social Anxiety Disorder (also termed Social Phobia in ICD-10), characterized by fear of social situations and performance in public, is the most likely diagnosis for someone using alcohol to manage anxiety during public speaking.

questions.question_text: A screening test is used in a population with low disease prevalence. How does low prevalence affect positive predictive value (PPV)?
questions.explanation: PPV decreases when prevalence is low because there are more false positives relative to true positives. NPV increases with low prevalence.

questions.question_text: Hypochondriasis is characterized by which of the following?

options.text: Abnormal preoccupation with health and fear of disease despite physical evidence to the contrary
Primary belief that symptoms are psychological
Significant functional impairment exclusively from physical symptoms

correct_answer.text: Abnormal preoccupation with health and fear of disease despite physical evidence to the contrary

questions.explanation: Hypochondriasis involves abnormal preoccupation with one's health and a fear of having or acquiring a disease despite physical evidence to the contrary, now classified under OCD and related disorders in ICD-11.

questions.question_text: A forest plot from a meta-analysis shows the mean difference between two treatments with error bars. What do the horizontal lines extending from each study's point estimate typically represent?
questions.explanation: In forest plots, the horizontal lines represent the 95% confidence interval for each study's effect estimate.

questions.question_text: A chronic alcoholic is telling stories with no link. What one occurs in confabulation?
questions.explanation: Confabulation is the unconscious creation of false memories to fill gaps in autobiographical memory. In chronic alcoholics with Korsakoff syndrome, patients unconsciously fill memory gaps with fabricated information without intent to deceive, resulting in disconnected stories.

questions.question_text: A homeless man presents with confusion, unstable gait, and diplopia. What should be administered first?
questions.explanation: Thiamine should be given before glucose in suspected Wernicke's encephalopathy to prevent precipitation of symptoms; the clinical presentation suggests thiamine deficiency.

questions.question_text: An ASD screening questionnaire correctly identifies ASD symptoms but shows no correlation with ADHD symptoms. What type of validity does this demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Divergent validity shows a measure does NOT correlate with measures of different constructs - ASD scale shouldn't correlate with ADHD.

questions.question_text: What function is preserved in normal aging?
questions.explanation: Spatial abilities tend to be relatively preserved during normal aging, whereas working memory, processing speed, and episodic memory typically decline with age.

questions.question_text: What is the current estimated number of people aged over 65 years in the UK?
questions.explanation: The source clearly states that 10 million people in the UK are over 65 years old, representing one sixth of the population. This is a straightforward factual recall question. ---

questions.question_text: What percentage of people experience delirium in the week after a stroke?
questions.explanation: Evidence shows: Delirium affects 30-40% of people in the week after a stroke. This is a specific epidemiological fact presented in the cerebrovascular disease section. The other percentage ranges do not match this specification. ---

questions.question_text: What cognitive outcome is associated with volunteering for 100 or more hours per year in older adults?
questions.explanation: Volunteering for 100 hours or more per year is associated with older adults having more positive self-perceptions of aging and fewer depressive symptoms, which subsequently predicts reduced dementia risk.

questions.question_text: What is a key advantage of conducting new assessments of older people at their home?

options.text: Depth and quality of information, and avoidance of a potentially tiring and expensive journey
Easier access to physical examination equipment

correct_answer.text: Depth and quality of information, and avoidance of a potentially tiring and expensive journey

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states: There are many advantages to undertaking new assessments at the patient's home, particularly for people with dementia – depth and quality of information, and avoidance of a potentially tiring and expensive journey for patients. While other options may have some merit, only this one is specifically mentioned in the source material. ---

questions.question_text: Everybody's Business (2005) clarified that older people's mental health problems require input from which combination of services?

options.text: Both health and social care, physical and mental health services, mainstream and specialist services
Primary care and voluntary services only

correct_answer.text: Both health and social care, physical and mental health services, mainstream and specialist services

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that Everybody's Business (2005) clarified that older people's mental health problems require input from both health and social care, physical and mental health services and mainstream and specialist services. The other options are too restrictive and do not reflect the integrated approach described. ---

questions.question_text: What key concern has been raised about recent trends toward ageless services in some UK areas?

options.text: They reduce costs to the NHS
They improve patient outcomes across all age groups
They potentially breach the Equality Act 2010 by causing indirect discrimination and reducing patient choice
They are supported by the JCPMH commissioning guidance
They eliminate the need for specialist geriatricians

correct_answer.text: They potentially breach the Equality Act 2010 by causing indirect discrimination and reducing patient choice

questions.explanation: These changes have been highlighted as potentially breaching the Equality Act 2010 by causing indirect discrimination and reducing patient choice. The other options either contradict the source or misrepresent the service development concerns. ---

questions.question_text: Recent changes in UK older adults' mental health services involving a shift toward ageless services have been highlighted as potentially breaching which legislation?

options.text: The Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards Act

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states These changes have been highlighted as potentially breaching the Equality Act 2010 by causing indirect discrimination and reducing patient choice. This is a factual statement about the specific legislation referenced. ---

questions.question_text: Which cognitive function is most consistently resilient in normal ageing?
questions.explanation: Working memory is often considered the most consistently resilient cognitive function in normal aging, maintaining relatively good functionality compared to other domains like selective attention and spatial orientation, although processing speed declines with age.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the Needs-Based Criteria for Older People's Mental Health Services developed by the Royal College of Psychiatrists?

options.text: Services should be based on age of the patient exclusively
Services should address people with functional illness and dementia, with consideration of comorbid physical illness and social difficulties related to ageing
Services should be provided only by primary care
Services should exclude people with multiple comorbidities

correct_answer.text: Services should address people with functional illness and dementia, with consideration of comorbid physical illness and social difficulties related to ageing

questions.explanation: The Needs-Based Criteria as including people of any age with primary dementia, people with mental disorder and physical illness/frailty, and those with psychological/social difficulties related to ageing. This reflects a holistic, needs-based approach. Option A is explicitly contradicted by the source's statement that Services must be commissioned on the basis of need and not age alone. ---

questions.question_text: According to the National Service Framework for Older People (2001), what was the key standard regarding older people with mental health problems?

options.text: They should be treated only in primary care settings
They should have access to specialist services
They should receive age-appropriate care from generic services only
They should be managed exclusively by geriatricians
They should have access to long-term care facilities

correct_answer.text: They should have access to specialist services

questions.explanation: The source directly states The National Service Framework for Older People (2001) contained a key standard that older people with mental health problems should have access to specialist services. The other options contradict this explicit standard or misrepresent the guidance. ---

questions.question_text: A 79-year-old woman with multiple comorbidities is being assessed for mental health service referral. According to JCPMH commissioning guidance, which approach to her care is most appropriate?

options.text: Refer only to geriatric medicine, not mental health
Refer to a youth mental health service
Ensure services work closely with social services, primary care, community services, and geriatricians
Provide specialist mental health services that work in isolation
Delay assessment until she reaches age 85

correct_answer.text: Ensure services work closely with social services, primary care, community services, and geriatricians

questions.explanation: Evidence emphasizes that JCPMH commissioning guidance stresses the need for close working with social services, primary care, community services, voluntary services and geriatricians. This integrated multidisciplinary approach is a fundamental principle. ---

questions.question_text: What percentage of carers of older people with mental health problems will suffer depression at some stage?
questions.explanation: The source directly states 30% of carers will suffer depression at some stage. This is a straightforward factual recall question about carer mental health outcomes. ---

questions.question_text: Which of the following about old age pharmacokinetics is true?

options.text: Absorption is increased compared to younger adults
Free drug concentration in plasma increases

correct_answer.text: Free drug concentration in plasma increases

questions.explanation: In elderly patients, there is increased free drug concentration in plasma due to decreased plasma protein binding and altered distribution, leading to increased drug effects.

questions.question_text: Which of the following metabolic or physiological changes can produce affective symptoms during illness?

options.text: Dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, endocrine changes, and infection

correct_answer.text: Dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, endocrine changes, and infection

questions.explanation: Metabolic changes during illness can accentuate the emotional response to it – dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, endocrine changes and infection can all produce affective symptoms. All four factors are listed as capable of producing affective symptoms. ---

questions.question_text: According to the source, specialist older adults services have recently experienced which trend in some areas of the UK?

options.text: Reduction with movement toward ageless services

correct_answer.text: Reduction with movement toward ageless services

questions.explanation: Evidence shows: There has been a recent trend of specialised older adults services being reduced and a movement to ageless services in some areas of the UK. This describes a significant service development change. Options A, C, D, and E either contradict this trend or are not mentioned in the source material. ---

questions.question_text: The post-stroke incidence of stroke related to antipsychotic use is approximately:
questions.explanation: Antipsychotics are associated with an approximately 1% increased risk of stroke; this risk is higher in elderly patients and with typical antipsychotics.

questions.question_text: Which cognitive domain is commonly affected in Parkinson's disease?

options.text: Higher executive dysfunction, attention, memory, visuomotor processing, and visual attention

correct_answer.text: Higher executive dysfunction, attention, memory, visuomotor processing, and visual attention

questions.explanation: The source lists higher executive dysfunction, attention, memory, visuomotor processing and visual attention as common cognitive deficits in PD. This reflects the multidomain cognitive impairment characteristic of PD-related cognitive changes, not isolated deficits. ---

questions.question_text: According to the source, what is the defining characteristic of adjustment disorders following physical illness?

options.text: By their nature they are transient
They always require long-term psychiatric treatment
They are resistant to all psychological interventions
They invariably lead to chronic depression

correct_answer.text: By their nature they are transient

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that Adjustment disorders are common following physical illness and by their nature are transient. This directly defines the temporal characteristic of adjustment disorders. ---

questions.question_text: The Everybody's Business framework (2005) emphasized that older people's mental health problems require input from which of the following?

options.text: Health and social care, physical and mental health services, mainstream and specialist services
Primary care physicians and psychiatrists only
Social services and voluntary organizations only

correct_answer.text: Health and social care, physical and mental health services, mainstream and specialist services

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that older people's mental health needs require input from both health and social care, physical and mental health services and mainstream and specialist services. This reflects an integrated, multidisciplinary approach. The other options represent incomplete or overly restrictive service provision models. ---

questions.question_text: Which consequence of child maltreatment demonstrates the broadest psychiatric impact?

options.text: Non-specific risk factor for multiple forms of psychopathology

correct_answer.text: Non-specific risk factor for multiple forms of psychopathology

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that child maltreatment is a non-specific risk factor for multiple forms of psychopathology, including PTSD, depression, eating disorders, oppositional defiant disorder, and conduct disorder.

questions.question_text: What can a 36-month-old child do regarding language?
questions.explanation: By 36 months, a child can understand grammatical syntax accurately, though they may not yet produce perfectly grammatical speech.

questions.question_text: A 15-year-old girl with a history of childhood sexual abuse now presents with depression, substance use, and deliberate self-harm. Which source statement best contextualises these presentations?

options.text: Adolescents with trauma history show affective disorders, substance abuse, anxiety disorders, and self-destructive behaviour
Indicates need for immediate hospitalisation regardless of risk assessment

correct_answer.text: Adolescents with trauma history show affective disorders, substance abuse, anxiety disorders, and self-destructive behaviour

questions.explanation: That adolescents affected by parental mental illness show Affective disorders (depression), anxiety disorders...substance abuse, and separately lists maltreatment victims as having increased rates of...depression, self-destructive behaviour. This case fits the predicted developmental trajectory.

questions.question_text: Which is not a risk factor for delayed speech impairment?
questions.explanation: Risk factors associated with delayed speech and language include family history, male gender, twins, lower maternal education, childhood illness, being born late in the family order, young mother at birth, and low socioeconomic status. Immigration status is not listed as an established risk factor, whereas the other options relate to environmental, genetic, or developmental factors known to impact speech development.

questions.question_text: An 18-month-old child in a care institution does not seek comfort from caregivers when injured. Which attachment disorder is this consistent with?
questions.explanation: Reactive attachment disorder is characterized by grossly abnormal attachment behaviours in early childhood in the context of inadequate care. The child does not turn to the primary caregiver for comfort and rarely displays security-seeking behaviours toward any adult.

questions.question_text: In Marcia's identity status framework, identity moratorium is characterized by which of the following?

options.text: Commitment to a choice without prior exploration

questions.explanation: Identity moratorium is characterized by active exploration without yet making a commitment. The individual is in the process of exploring various identities and values but has not yet committed to a particular identity.

questions.question_text: At which age does mid-life crisis occur?
questions.explanation: Mid-life crisis typically occurs during the middle adult stage, which spans ages 40-65 years, with the most common onset between 40 and 60 years of age.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the LEAST likely to cause delayed speech and language development?
questions.explanation: Immigration is not listed among the established risk factors for delayed speech and language development. Established risk factors include family history, male gender, twin status, lower maternal education, childhood illness, late birth order, young maternal age, and low socioeconomic status.

questions.question_text: In terms of reported cases, what percentage of child maltreatment involves neglect?
questions.explanation: That of reported cases, approximately 60% are for neglect, 20% for physical abuse, 10% for sexual abuse, and 10% for other forms of maltreatment.

questions.question_text: The source suggests that a child presenting repeatedly for medical attention may warrant evaluation for which form of maltreatment?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly cautions that clinicians need to be aware when a young person repeatedly presents for medical attention, as this may indicate factitious disorder by proxy, which can be difficult to detect.

questions.question_text: The effects of parental mental illness on children are best understood as:

options.text: Directly caused by genetic inheritance alone
Mediated by complex factors including direct exposure, parenting changes, and social/genetic variables
Invariably leading to identical psychiatric outcomes in all children
Preventable through pharmacological treatment of the parent alone

correct_answer.text: Mediated by complex factors including direct exposure, parenting changes, and social/genetic variables

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states It is important to note that the effects of parental mental illness on children are mediated by complex factors and then outlines Rutter's three-factor model including direct exposure, altered parenting, and mediator variables.

questions.question_text: In the source, emotional abuse is distinguished from other forms of maltreatment primarily by which characteristic?

options.text: Repeated messaging that the child is worthless, defective, or unwanted

correct_answer.text: Repeated messaging that the child is worthless, defective, or unwanted

questions.explanation: Emotional/psychological abuse as when an adult repeatedly conveys that a child is worthless, defective, flawed, unloved, or unwanted. This verbal/messaging component distinguishes it from physical abuse (A), sexual abuse (B), neglect (D), and factitious disorder (E).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true about bullying?

options.text: It is more common in girls than boys
Bullies prefer victims of the same type
It is less common in secondary school than primary school
It has no long-term psychological effects

questions.explanation: Bullies typically demonstrate lower social maturity, poorer impulse control, and deficient social skills compared to non-bullying peers.

questions.question_text: During the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex development in adolescence, which cognitive functions show the most significant improvement?

options.text: Higher-order cognitive functions such as complex decision-making and working memory

correct_answer.text: Higher-order cognitive functions such as complex decision-making and working memory

questions.explanation: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) undergoes significant development during adolescence and is responsible for higher-order cognitive functions, such as complex decision-making, reasoning, working memory, and planning.

questions.question_text: Physical abuse is best defined as:

options.text: Any act that causes emotional distress to a child
Intentional injury including beating, punching, kicking, burning, and poisoning
Exposure to parental violence without direct contact
Neglect of a child's basic needs

correct_answer.text: Intentional injury including beating, punching, kicking, burning, and poisoning

questions.explanation: Physical abuse as any act that results in a nonaccidental physical injury, such as beating, punching, kicking, biting, burning, and poisoning. This matches option B. A refers to emotional harm, C to exposure, D to neglect, and E to verbal abuse—all distinct categories.

questions.question_text: A clinical team is debating whether a 6-year-old with acute OCD and motor tics 4 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis meets criteria for PANDAS. Which diagnostic criterion is most critical to confirm this diagnosis versus idiopathic childhood OCD?

options.text: Presence of OCD or tic disorder
Temporal relationship of symptom onset/exacerbation to group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection

correct_answer.text: Temporal relationship of symptom onset/exacerbation to group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection

questions.explanation: While all five NIMH criteria are necessary for PANDAS diagnosis, criterion 4 (temporal relationship to GABHS infection) is the distinguishing feature separating PANDAS from idiopathic OCD with comorbid tics. Options A, B, and D are necessary but not sufficient (present in non-PANDAS cases); option E supports but does not confirm criterion 4. The temporal relationship is the mechanistic lynchpin distinguishing autoimmune-mediated PANDAS from genetic/sporadic OCD. ---

questions.question_text: Which psychiatric condition is NOT mentioned as a consequence of childhood sexual abuse?
questions.explanation: The source lists depression, PTSD, conduct disorders, somatisation, and suicidal behaviour in those with a history of sexual abuse. Schizophrenia is not mentioned as a consequence.

questions.question_text: Which consequence of maternal depression is most commonly observed in infants?

options.text: Anger and protective coping style with passivity and withdrawal
Reduced adaptive functioning and affective disorders

correct_answer.text: Anger and protective coping style with passivity and withdrawal

questions.explanation: The source explicitly lists Anger and protective style of coping, passivity, withdrawal, reduced attention and lower IQ as effects on infants. Aggression and conduct problems are more typical in toddlers and school-age children. Anxiety disorders and phobias emerge in adolescence. Substance abuse appears in adolescence, not infancy.

questions.question_text: What is the maximum duration for which Section 35 (remand for report on mental state) can be renewed in total?
questions.explanation: Section 35 is used for a limited period, e.g., 28 days, up to a maximum of 12 weeks total. This timeframe is specifically stated in the source and reflects the assessment purpose of the section. ---

questions.question_text: In very serious cases where a hospital order has been given by Crown Court with no time limit on the order, which additional section has been applied?
questions.explanation: A restriction order (Section 41) can be added to a hospital order and has no time limit. Without restriction, a hospital order lasts initially for six months and is renewable. Section 47 is for transfer from prison to hospital, and Section 49 is a restriction direction applied to Section 47. Section 38 is an interim hospital order. ---

questions.question_text: A driving licensing authority reviews psychiatric conditions associated with increased risk of road traffic accidents and dangerous driving behavior. Which condition is most strongly associated with dangerous driving?
questions.explanation: Substance misuse is the leading medical cause for licence revocation and is most strongly linked to dangerous violations like speeding and road rage. It directly and immediately impairs driving ability affecting reaction time, judgment, and coordination, and accounts for a significant proportion of road traffic accidents and fatalities.

questions.question_text: An offender is placed under supervision with a focus on support and treatment via a social worker. Which disposal order is being used?
questions.explanation: A supervision order allows an individual to receive support and treatment, usually with the aid of a social worker. This differs from guardianship orders, which emphasize care and protection, and absolute discharge, which requires no further action.

questions.question_text: A court remands an offender to hospital for assessment of substance misuse and mental health. Which section is being used?
questions.explanation: Section 35 is the remand for report on mental state, typically lasting 28 days up to a maximum of 12 weeks. Section 36 is also for remand to hospital for treatment (rarely used), while Section 37 is a hospital order following conviction. Sections 47 and 48 relate to transfer of sentenced prisoners.

questions.question_text: Which factor determines whether an offender receives bail or remand into custody after initial arrest?

options.text: Severity of offence amongst other factors

correct_answer.text: Severity of offence amongst other factors

questions.explanation: After the first hearing, individuals can be bailed into the community or remanded into custody depending on the severity of the offence, amongst other factors. Mental disorder alone does not determine bail; it is one consideration among many in assessing risk and need.

questions.question_text: An offender is detained under Section 37 without restriction and requests conditional discharge after 8 months. Who has the authority to approve this?

options.text: Responsible Clinician (hospital managers have authority for unrestricted sections)

correct_answer.text: Responsible Clinician (hospital managers have authority for unrestricted sections)

questions.explanation: For a Section 37 hospital order without restriction, the Responsible Clinician and hospital managers have discharge authority (absolutely or conditionally). The Ministry of Justice permission is required only for restricted orders (Section 41). After 8 months, renewal and discharge decisions fall within normal hospital order authority. --- **SUMMARY OF DIFFICULTY DISTRIBUTION:** - **Easy (1-Step, 40%):** Questions 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 22, 24, 27 (16 questions) - **Medium (2-Step, 30%):** Questions 1, 7, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 21, 25, 28, 30, 32 (12 questions) - **Difficult (3-Step, 30%):** Questions 23, 26, 29, 31, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40 (12 questions) **STEM TYPE DISTRIBUTION:** - **Fact-Focus/Short Stems (60%):** 24 questions - **Case Vignettes (10%):** 4 questions - **Incomplete Statements (30%):** 12 questions

questions.question_text: An interim hospital order (Section 38) is best understood as serving which primary function?

options.text: Assessment period before deciding on final disposal

correct_answer.text: Assessment period before deciding on final disposal

questions.explanation: An interim hospital order represents an assessment period before determining the most appropriate final disposal. It allows the court to gather additional information about treatability and risk before committing to a permanent hospital order. ---

questions.question_text: The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) in England and Wales decides whether to continue prosecution based primarily on:

options.text: Whether public interest outweighs other concerns

correct_answer.text: Whether public interest outweighs other concerns

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states the CPS decides if the prosecution should continue. The CPS continue prosecution if the public interest outweighs any other concerns. Public interest is the formal criterion. While severity, psychiatric history, and victim input may inform this judgment, the explicit standard is balancing public interest against other factors.

questions.question_text: A sentenced prisoner is transferred to hospital via Section 47 for treatment of acute psychosis. Six months later, the sentence expires. Which action reflects the correct legal process?

options.text: Section 49 restriction is removed; Section is notionally converted to Section 37

correct_answer.text: Section 49 restriction is removed; Section is notionally converted to Section 37

questions.explanation: The source explicitly describes this scenario: Section 49 restriction is removed at sentence expiry, and the Section is converted notionally to Section 37, allowing continued psychiatric care without custodial restriction but with RC and renewal safeguards. Options A (no legal safeguard), B (no psychiatric care), D (incorrect section application), and E (not the statutory pathway) are incorrect.

questions.question_text: Detention schools differ from Young Offender Institutes in that detention schools have:
questions.explanation: Detention schools, in general, have higher relational security than YOIs. The source explicitly makes this comparison. This distinction reflects different management approaches and intensity of supervision, with detention schools providing more intensive relational/supervisory security than YOIs.

questions.question_text: The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) in England and Wales decides whether to continue prosecution based on which criterion?

options.text: The severity of the crime alone
Whether public interest outweighs other concerns
The recommendation of the defence solicitor
The prior criminal history of the offender

correct_answer.text: Whether public interest outweighs other concerns

questions.explanation: That the CPS decides if prosecution should continue if public interest outweighs any other concerns. While severity may be considered, the explicit criterion given is the balance of public interest. The other options are not stated as the CPS's decision-making criterion.

questions.question_text: Which of the following psychiatric conditions shows increased prevalence with greater severity of learning disability?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly identifies schizophrenia as one of the mental health problems where the greater the severity of LD, the higher the risk of mental health problems. The other options are not mentioned as being severity-correlated in the source.

questions.question_text: A patient with an IQ of 28 and requiring assistance with most aspects of daily living would be classified as having which severity of learning disability?
questions.explanation: An IQ of 28 falls within the profound range (<20 is the threshold, but Evidence indicates profound includes the lowest functioning individuals). The requirement for assistance with most ADL further confirms profound LD. The profound category is explicitly defined as <20, but given the context of needing comprehensive care and the IQ being substantially below 20, this indicates profound LD. ---

questions.question_text: What is the key difference in occupational potential between individuals with moderate and severe learning disability?

options.text: Moderate: may achieve self-maintenance in unskilled or semiskilled work with support; Severe: may perform work-related tasks under supervision but cannot achieve self-maintenance through work
Only severe LD individuals can work
Moderate LD individuals cannot work; severe LD individuals can

correct_answer.text: Moderate: may achieve self-maintenance in unskilled or semiskilled work with support; Severe: may perform work-related tasks under supervision but cannot achieve self-maintenance through work

questions.explanation: That moderate LD individuals may achieve self-maintenance in unskilled or semiskilled work with appropriate support and supervision, whereas those with severe LD may be able to perform work-related tasks under supervision but adapted to supervised living situations, implying lesser occupational independence.

questions.question_text: Which psychiatric condition is particularly highly prevalent in individuals with severe learning disability?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that individuals with severe learning disability have a particularly high rate of autism spectrum disorder and pervasive developmental disorder, in contrast to those with mild learning disability who show higher rates of conduct disorder.

questions.question_text: Rubella infection during pregnancy is classified as which type of aetiological factor for learning disability?
questions.explanation: The source categorises prenatal infections such as rubella, cytomegalovirus, syphilis, toxoplasmosis, herpes simplex virus and HIV infections as external prenatal factors, particularly when they occur in early stages of pregnancy.

questions.question_text: A 9-year-old boy presents with intellectual disability, autism spectrum features, and physical examination revealing macroorchidism, large prominent ears, and a long face with prominent jaw. Which genetic syndrome is most likely?
questions.explanation: Fragile X syndrome presents with large ears, long face, macroorchidism, intellectual disability, and autism features.

questions.question_text: Which aetiological category includes Down's syndrome?
questions.explanation: The source lists autosomal chromosome disorders as including Down's syndrome. Sex chromosome disorders are separate, as are X-linked conditions and mitochondrial disorders.

questions.question_text: Health inequalities experienced by people with learning disability stem from which of the following factors?

options.text: Biological inferiority of people with LD
Barriers to accessing timely, appropriate and effective health care
Natural shorter lifespan unrelated to health service factors

correct_answer.text: Barriers to accessing timely, appropriate and effective health care

questions.explanation: That people with LD have poorer health than the general population and these health inequalities can stem from barriers they face in accessing timely, appropriate and effective health care, identifying systemic barriers rather than individual limitations as the cause.

questions.question_text: How is the term 'learning difficulty' distinguished from 'learning disability' according to the source?

options.text: Learning difficulty refers to conditions such as dyslexia and dyspraxia
Learning disability is only used in the USA
Learning difficulty is more severe than learning disability
They apply to different age groups

correct_answer.text: Learning difficulty refers to conditions such as dyslexia and dyspraxia

questions.explanation: That the term 'learning difficulty' has often been used interchangeably with 'learning disability' but specifies Learning difficulties is the term used to refer to difficulties such as dyslexia and dyspraxia, distinguishing them as separate concepts.

questions.question_text: A four-year-old boy who was born in India presents with epilepsy, severe mental retardation and behavioural problems. On examination, you note the lack of pigment in skin and hair. The diagnosis is
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of hypopigmentation (fair skin, blond hair), seizures, severe intellectual disability, and behavioral problems is characteristic of untreated Phenylketonuria. PKU is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency. The hypopigmentation occurs because phenylalanine is required for melanin synthesis. Untreated patients develop seizures in 25% of cases, severe intellectual disability, and the characteristic musty or mouse-like odor.

questions.question_text: A person with profound learning disability has comorbid seizure disorder. According to the epidemiological data, what is the maximum expected prevalence of psychiatric comorbidity in this scenario?
questions.explanation: That psychiatric disorders in individuals with LD and neurological conditions may be as high as 50% in those with profound LD, indicating 50% is the upper estimate provided for this high-risk group.

questions.question_text: According to the source, what is the relationship between severity of learning disability and risk of mental health problems?

options.text: Mild learning disability carries the highest risk
The greater the severity of learning disability, the higher the risk
Risk is only present in moderate learning disability

correct_answer.text: The greater the severity of learning disability, the higher the risk

questions.explanation: The epidemiology section clearly states that the prevalence of psychopathology seems to be correlated with the severity of LD; the greater the severity of LD, the higher the risk of mental health problems. This includes mood disorders, schizophrenia, ADHD, and conduct disorder.

questions.question_text: According to Freud's structural model, the ego functions primarily as which of the following?

options.text: The source of instinctual and sexual impulses
The seat of internalised moral values and conscience
The executive organ of the mind linked with reality
The unconscious repository of repressed conflicts
The mediator between the individual's fantasies and internal desires

correct_answer.text: The executive organ of the mind linked with reality

questions.explanation: The ego is explicitly described as the executive organ of the mind linked with reality. Option A describes the id. Option B describes the superego. Option D describes the unconscious aspects of the id. Option E, while partially related to the ego's function, is less precise than the definition of it as the executive organ.

questions.question_text: Triangulation in family systems theory refers to:

options.text: Involvement of a third party to reduce tension between two members

correct_answer.text: Involvement of a third party to reduce tension between two members

questions.explanation: Triangulation occurs when tension between two family members is managed by involving a third member, often an unhealthy family dynamic.

questions.question_text: According to Freud's theory of dreams, which component includes unconscious thoughts, wishes, and the residues from daily experience?
questions.explanation: Latent content is specifically defined as comprising unconscious mental matter (thoughts, wishes), residues from the day, and stimuli experienced during sleep. Manifest content is what is recalled. Dream work is the process transforming latent into manifest. Evidence shows this exact definition in the diagram.

questions.question_text: Condensation in dreamwork involves which of the following?

options.text: One unconscious impulse represented by several images
Two or more unconscious impulses combined into a single image
Energy invested in one idea transferred to another
An innocent image substituted for an overwhelming fantasy
The transformation of manifest content into latent content

correct_answer.text: Two or more unconscious impulses combined into a single image

questions.explanation: Condensation is explicitly defined as two or more unconscious impulses being combined into a single image, exemplified by a strict father and punitive teacher combining into one frightening monster. Option A describes diffusion/irradiation. Option C describes displacement. Option D describes symbolic representation. Option E reverses the direction of dreamwork.

questions.question_text: Melanie Klein's concept of the depressive position involves which developmental achievement?

options.text: Fear of retaliation from the bad object
Retreat and cutting off from others
Integration of good and bad aspects and development of guilt and wish to repair
Formation of the superego through identification

correct_answer.text: Integration of good and bad aspects and development of guilt and wish to repair

questions.explanation: The depressive position is specifically described as occurring once an infant can integrate good and bad qualities in the mother (seeing her as having both), leading to feelings of guilt and a wish to repair any damage caused. This represents developmental progress from the paranoid-schizoid position's splitting.

questions.question_text: What does the Q Sort test measure in psychology?
questions.explanation: The Q Sort test is used to study people's subjectivity and viewpoint. It uses factor analysis to understand how people think about an issue and can be used in both clinical and research settings.

questions.question_text: A therapist using Rogers' client-centered approach while incorporating Beck's cognitive model would most appropriately employ which therapeutic technique?
questions.explanation: When Rogerian person-centered principles are incorporated with Beck's cognitive model, the resulting approach is cognitive therapy, which combines the therapeutic relationship and acceptance of Rogers with the structured cognitive techniques of Beck.

questions.question_text: Individuation, in Jung's analytical psychology, refers to which developmental process?

options.text: The process in which an individual develops self-identity
Integration of the personal and collective unconscious

correct_answer.text: The process in which an individual develops self-identity

questions.explanation: Individuation is specifically defined as the process in which the individual develops self-identity. This is Jung's central concept of psychological development, involving integration of conscious and unconscious aspects including the persona, shadow, anima/animus, and self.

questions.question_text: During a CBT session, a patient says I'm terrible at my job; I made a mistake yesterday. The therapist responds: Why don't we see this as an opportunity to learn rather than evidence you're terrible? Which CBT technique is the therapist using?
questions.explanation: Reframing restructures negative interpretations into alternative, more adaptive perspectives.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic approach involves reflecting on how intended outcomes are affected by current behaviors?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing is a counseling method that helps people resolve ambivalent feelings and insecurities to find internal motivation for behavior change, considering the difficulty of making life changes. It involves reflecting on discrepancies between current behaviors and desired outcomes. While Rogerian therapy uses reflection, motivational interviewing specifically focuses on exploring the gap between current behavior and intended outcomes.

questions.question_text: Which theory describes the stages of grief including protest, despair, and detachment?
questions.explanation: Bowlby's attachment and grief theory describes protest, despair, and detachment as stages in the grief and loss response.

questions.question_text: In Freud's structural model, which component is primarily unconscious and contains sexual and aggressive impulses?
questions.explanation: The id is specifically defined as full of instinctual aspects including sexual and aggressive impulses, and is mostly unconscious. The ego is the executive linked to reality. The superego contains internalized morals. Persona and anima are Jungian concepts.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old woman with a 10-year history of bipolar I disorder is planning pregnancy. She is currently stable on lithium monotherapy. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management strategy?

options.text: Maintain lithium throughout pregnancy without dose adjustment
Consider dosage reduction and regular review, maintaining treatment given high relapse risk
Switch to valproate as a safer alternative in pregnancy

correct_answer.text: Consider dosage reduction and regular review, maintaining treatment given high relapse risk

questions.explanation: The source recommends that patients with severe illness and high risk of relapse should be maintained on medication, with maintenance strategies involve dosage reduction and regular review of side effects. Abrupt discontinuation risks relapse (8-fold increased risk in first month postpartum); valproate is explicitly contraindicated; switching without stabilisation is unsafe. This requires linking clinical severity, relapse risk, and management principles.

questions.question_text: During which weeks of pregnancy are organs at greatest risk for major morphological teratogenic effects from medications?
questions.explanation: Teratogenic effects are both dose and time dependent, with organs at the greatest risk during their period of fastest development. Week 6 to week 10 is the most vulnerable period. This critical window defines timing for medication avoidance and informed decision-making about risk–benefit analysis in early pregnancy.

questions.question_text: What is a major risk of valproate exposure in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Valproate causes neural tube defects and significantly increases the risk of autism spectrum disorder and developmental delay (fetal valproate syndrome).

questions.question_text: Which is true about Clozapine in pregnancy?

options.text: Dose needs increasing due to enzyme induction
Dose needs increasing due to increased GFR
Dose reduction required due to enzyme inhibition by oestrogens
Can be safely discontinued without taper

correct_answer.text: Dose needs increasing due to increased GFR

questions.explanation: During pregnancy, increased glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and renal clearance occur, along with increased volume of distribution and induced liver metabolic pathways. These changes typically necessitate dose increases of medications like clozapine to maintain therapeutic levels.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true about Clozapine use in pregnancy?

options.text: Dose needs increasing due to enzyme induction
Dose needs increasing due to increased GFR
Dose reduction is required due to enzyme inhibition by estrogens
It has no effect on pregnancy outcomes

correct_answer.text: Dose needs increasing due to increased GFR

questions.explanation: During pregnancy, increased glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and renal clearance occur due to physiological changes. Additionally, induced liver metabolic pathways and increased volume of distribution result in lower drug concentrations, necessitating dose increases to maintain therapeutic levels.

questions.question_text: What is the risk of congenital anomalies associated with valproate exposure during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Valproate exposure during pregnancy is associated with congenital anomalies in 8-12% of exposed pregnancies, along with developmental delays in 31-40%.

questions.question_text: Valproate-induced congenital anomalies occur in approximately what percentage of exposed pregnancies?
questions.explanation: Valproate carries a risk of congenital anomalies in 8-12% of exposed pregnancies, along with developmental delays in 31-40%.

questions.question_text: What is the risk of postpartum psychosis in the general population?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states The risk of postpartum psychosis is 0.1–0.25% in general population. All other percentages either fall outside this range or represent risk in specific populations (such as bipolar disorder at 50%).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a fetal malformation associated with sodium valproate exposure?

options.text: Limb defects including aplasia of radius

questions.explanation: Sodium valproate is associated with neural tube defects (1-4%), facial dysmorphism, cleft lip and palate (1-2%), craniostenosis, cardiac, renal, urogenital, and limb defects, but micrognathia is not a typical valproate-associated malformation.

questions.question_text: A 1-10 year old child presents with cleft palate and delayed milestones. Which medication exposure during pregnancy is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Sodium valproate is a known teratogen associated with fetal valproate syndrome, which includes cleft palate and neurodevelopmental delay including delayed milestones.

questions.question_text: An epidemiologist observes that countries with low religious attachment have high suicide rates, then concludes that low religious attachment CAUSES high suicide rates in individuals. What is this reasoning error called?
questions.explanation: The ecological fallacy is the erroneous assumption that group-level associations apply to individuals within those groups. The source explicitly illustrates this error: countries with low religious attachment may have high suicide rates, but individual suicide victims may or may not be religious. Drawing individual-level conclusions from group-level data defines ecological fallacy. The other options describe different types of bias not applicable here. ---

questions.question_text: Which statistical method is used to measure publication bias in meta-analyses?
questions.explanation: A funnel plot is the primary graphical method used to detect publication bias in meta-analyses by displaying asymmetry that suggests missing small negative studies.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best explains the ecological fallacy?

options.text: Estimates of effect at the ecological group level do not equate to biological effects at the individual level
Ecological studies cannot be conducted efficiently using existing data
Ecological studies are always more expensive than individual-level studies
Correlations found in groups always apply to individuals within those groups
Ecological studies cannot identify any associations between variables

correct_answer.text: Estimates of effect at the ecological group level do not equate to biological effects at the individual level

questions.explanation: The source explicitly defines ecological fallacy as: Estimates of effect at the ecological level do not equate to estimates of biological effect obtained from individual level analysis. This is the core limitation of inferring individual causality from group-level correlations. Option D contradicts this concept; the other options misrepresent ecological study characteristics.

questions.question_text: In a case-control study, selecting cases from multiple sources (hospital, clinic, community) while selecting controls from a single source introduces which type of error?
questions.explanation: Controls must be recruited from the same source population as cases. Selecting cases from multiple sources but controls from one source means controls are not representative of the population from which all cases arose, creating selection bias. ---

questions.question_text: A forest plot shows multiple studies with different sized squares representing each study's point estimate. Which study contributes most weight to the overall meta-analysis result?
questions.explanation: Square size represents study weight; larger square means greater contribution to pooled estimate.

questions.question_text: Which study design would be most appropriate to answer the question What is the effect of this intervention?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly lists Pragmatic RCT (or systematic reviews) as the best study design to answer questions about treatment effectiveness and intervention effects. Case-control studies assess causation retrospectively, not intervention effects. Cross-sectional studies provide snapshots, and case reports lack comparison groups.

questions.question_text: Which statistical test would be used to compare non-parametric data across groups?
questions.explanation: Mann-Whitney U test is the non-parametric alternative to the independent t-test, used for comparing two groups of non-parametric data.

questions.question_text: A consultant asks you to complete an audit on prescribing nicotine replacement therapy for new inpatients. You identify the Trust's Drug & Therapeutics Guideline as the gold standard and collect the data. You then present it to your consultant colleagues. Six months later you reaudit the process to determine if there has been an improvement. What important aspect of the audit process has been omitted?

options.text: Publishing the results in a peer-reviewed journal
Presenting the findings at a national level
Initiating change after the first cycle

correct_answer.text: Initiating change after the first cycle

questions.explanation: Before re-auditing, one must implement changes to see if they have made a difference. The audit cycle requires implementing interventions based on findings before conducting a second cycle to assess improvement.

questions.question_text: The main disadvantage of qualitative studies regarding attitudes and behaviors is which of the following?

options.text: Attitudes expressed may not reflect actual behaviors
They are limited to psychiatric populations

correct_answer.text: Attitudes expressed may not reflect actual behaviors

questions.explanation: Evidence shows that qualitative studies are prone to observation and measurement bias, and that attitudes may not reflect behaviors; the information provided by participants may not reflect their actual behaviors. This represents a validity concern rather than cost, design, or scope limitations.

questions.question_text: The forced swim test is used to assess which condition?
questions.explanation: The forced swim test is an animal model used to assess learned helplessness and is related to depression, as it measures despair-like behavior in response to inescapable stress.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman who is pregnant asks about the risk of Down syndrome at her age. What is the approximate risk at age 40?
questions.explanation: Risk of Down syndrome at maternal age 40 is approximately 1:100.

questions.question_text: An esketamine study showed improved QALYs of 0.07 at costs of 16,600 (community) and 16,900 (hospital). Which statement is true?

options.text: Esketamine was more expensive and not effective
A DEAR curve must be examined before making a decision
The cost-effectiveness ratio must be compared to willingness-to-pay threshold

correct_answer.text: The cost-effectiveness ratio must be compared to willingness-to-pay threshold

questions.explanation: The ICER (cost per QALY gained) must be compared to the willingness-to-pay threshold to determine cost-effectiveness; without this threshold, no conclusion can be drawn.

questions.question_text: A clinical trial testing the efficacy of a novel antidepressant under controlled conditions with strict inclusion/exclusion criteria would be best classified as which type?
questions.explanation: The source distinguishes experimental RCTs (testing efficacy under controlled conditions with strict criteria) from pragmatic RCTs (testing effectiveness in real-world settings). The description matches experimental design. Options C-E are not interventional studies. ---

questions.question_text: In a case-control study of schizophrenia, overzealous matching of controls to cases on variables such as educational attainment may result in which unintended consequence?

options.text: Difficulty in recruiting controls and reduced risk difference between groups

correct_answer.text: Difficulty in recruiting controls and reduced risk difference between groups

questions.explanation: That overzealous matching may not only make recruitment of controls difficult but can also reduce the risk difference between the two groups. Additionally, overzealous matching may inadvertently result in matching for putative causal factors as well, further obscuring associations.

questions.question_text: A clinical audit examines whether antipsychotic prescriptions in a psychiatric unit adhere to NICE guidelines. The audit finds that 95% of prescriptions meet the specified criteria. What is the major limitation of concluding from this audit that prescribing in this unit is of high quality?

options.text: The audit sample size was too small
Adherence to criteria does not necessarily equate to high quality or effectiveness
There was no control group for comparison
The audit did not measure patient outcomes

correct_answer.text: Adherence to criteria does not necessarily equate to high quality or effectiveness

questions.explanation: Evidence shows a key limitation of clinical audit: Because things have been done as per criteria

questions.question_text: In medical ethics, choosing a treatment option that benefits the greatest number of people would primarily reflect which ethical principle?
questions.explanation: Utilitarianism emphasizes maximizing overall benefit and selecting actions that produce the greatest good for the greatest number of people.
